passage:
Kashish,
I'm writing this because I can't say it properly out loud. I'm sorry for Saturday. When you asked if I wanted to come to the fair, I snapped "Stop asking me stuff!" and slammed the door. You didn't deserve that.
I don't even know why I was angry. One minute I was fine and then everything felt too loud. It keeps happening this year. Mummy says a lot of it is growing up, and to talk to the doctor if it gets too much, which I might.
What I'm trying now is to say "give me ten minutes" instead of snapping. It worked twice this week.
Can we go to the fair next week instead? I'll buy the candyfloss.
Nikita

qa.q: What did Nikita snap at Kashish?
qa.a: Nikita snapped "Stop asking me stuff!" and slammed the door.

qa.q: What does Nikita mean by "everything felt too loud"?
qa.a: Nikita is describing a sudden wave of irritation that came unchosen and can't be fully explained, which is confusing.

qa.q: Why is saying "give me ten minutes" a good step for Nikita?
qa.a: It gives Nikita space to let the mood pass without hurting someone, and tells others what is needed.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Kashish will probably feel relieved and understood, knowing the snap wasn't really about Kashish, and happy about the fair plan. 🤍

grounding: A teen writes an apology showing an understanding of sudden moods and choosing a better way to act.

passage: You're recording? Okay. I'm Kunal. I used to think I was just an angry person. Like, this year my younger cousin Bhupen came to stay, and he's nice, but everything he did annoyed me. The way he chewed. The way he said "bro." I'd feel this heat rising and I'd say something mean. Then later I'd feel awful and not know why I said it. My dad said he was the same at my age and that the moods pass, but I still have to choose what I do. So now when the heat comes, I go to the terrace for a bit. Sometimes I put on music. Bhupen and I actually play carrom now. I still get annoyed by the chewing though. That hasn't changed.

qa.q: Where does Kunal go when the heat rises?
qa.a: Kunal goes to the terrace for a bit.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel after saying something mean to Bhupen?
qa.a: Kunal felt awful and confused about the mean words, which shows the anger didn't match Kunal's real feelings about Bhupen.

qa.q: Why is going to the terrace a useful habit for Kunal?
qa.a: It gives Kunal a pause between the feeling and the action, so the mood can pass without Kunal hurting Bhupen.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have seen Kunal before the change?
qa.a: He probably felt unwelcome and confused, not knowing why his cousin kept snapping at small things like chewing.

grounding: A teen describes sudden irritability and choosing to step away rather than lash out.

passage: My brother Varun turned fifteen in March, and since then I've been living with a weather forecast I can't read. I'm Kavitha, his older sister. Some evenings he tells us jokes at dinner. Other evenings he slams his plate down because the rice is "too wet." Last Tuesday, Mummy asked about his homework, and he shouted. Then, a minute later, he came back from his room. His ears were red. "Sorry," he mumbled. "I'm just... I don't know." He went to fill the water bottles, which is his job, without being asked. I don't know what goes on in his head. But I've noticed he comes back faster now. Mummy says to give him room and not tease. I'm trying, though it's hard.

qa.q: What did Varun complain about the rice?
qa.a: He said it was "too wet."

qa.q: What might Varun's red ears suggest when he came back?
qa.a: They suggest he felt embarrassed and sorry about shouting, even though he couldn't explain his mood.

qa.q: How could the family support Varun during his mood swings?
qa.a: They could give him space in the moment, as Mummy says, and notice when he chooses to come back and repair things.

qa.q: What is it like for Kavitha to live with Varun's changing moods?
qa.a: It feels unpredictable and sometimes hard, but she's trying to be patient and notices small improvements.

grounding: A sister observes a teen's sudden irritability and his growing choice to return and repair.

passage: Monday: Sudha, fourteen, came home and her little sister Damini asked to borrow her pencil box. 'Why do you always TAKE my things?' Sudha shouted, and slammed the door. Later she felt awful and didn't know why she had exploded. Thursday: Sudha started a note on her phone: 'Moods.' She wrote down when she'd snapped. Hungry after school. Tired. Too many tests. She noticed it came in waves, often from nowhere. Mummy said her body was changing a lot and it was common, but she could still choose what to do. The next Tuesday: Damini peeked in. Sudha felt the heat rise. 'Dami, I'm in a mood. Give me ten minutes. Not about you.' After a snack, she called Damini back to play ludo.

qa.q: What did Damini ask to borrow on Monday?
qa.a: Sudha's pencil box.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel after slamming the door on Monday?
qa.a: She felt awful and confused about why she had exploded over something small.

qa.q: What did Sudha do on Tuesday that could help other teens with sudden moods?
qa.a: She named her mood, asked for a short break and explained it wasn't the other person's fault.

qa.q: How might Damini experience the difference between Monday and Tuesday?
qa.a: On Monday she felt shouted at for nothing, but on Tuesday she knew it wasn't about her and got to play later. 🙂

grounding: Shows a teen noticing sudden irritable moods and choosing how to act despite them.

passage: Jeevan, you slammed your door three times this week. No, I'm not scolding. I'll tell you about me at fourteen. One minute I'd be laughing with my friends, and the next I'd want to throw my books out of the window. I once shouted at my father because the dal was too salty, then cried in the bathroom, not knowing why. My mother said, 'Rashmi, your body is changing, the storms will come. You can't stop the rain, but you can hold the umbrella.' She taught me to go for a walk around the building before saying anything. It didn't always work. But more often, by the end of the walk, the storm had passed. Want to walk with me now?

qa.q: What did young Rashmi shout at her father about?
qa.a: That the dal was too salty.

qa.q: How did young Rashmi feel after shouting at her father?
qa.a: She felt confused and upset, crying in the bathroom without knowing why.

qa.q: What does Rashmi suggest Jeevan try when a mood hits?
qa.a: Walking around the building before saying anything, to let the storm pass.

qa.q: What might Jeevan feel when Rashmi says this is not a scolding?
qa.a: Jeevan might feel relieved and understood, and more willing to talk about those moods.

grounding: An elder recalls teenage mood shifts and a strategy for choosing how to act despite them.

passage:
The school bus broke down on the highway in the May heat, and for an hour the students of Class 9 sat sweating on the roadside.
Pallavi, fourteen, had woken up in a bad mood and didn't know why. When her best friend Zainab offered her a sip of water, Pallavi snapped, “Leave me alone! You're always fussing.”
Zainab's face fell. She moved to sit with someone else.
Pallavi sat alone, feeling awful. She'd been angry at nothing all week. Crying at adverts, shouting at her brother.
When the replacement bus came, she sat next to Zainab. “Sorry. I'm weird this week. It's not you.”
Zainab handed her the water bottle again. “I know. Mine was last month.”

qa.q: What did Zainab offer Pallavi?
qa.a: A sip of water.

qa.q: How was Pallavi feeling that week?
qa.a: She felt irritable and moody, angry at nothing, crying at adverts and shouting at her brother.

qa.q: What did Pallavi do that showed she could choose how to act despite her mood?
qa.a: She recognised her snapping wasn't about Zainab and apologised.

qa.q: How did Zainab react to the apology?
qa.a: She understood and forgave her, sharing that she had felt the same last month.

grounding: On a hot, stressful day a fourteen-year-old notices a sudden mood and repairs how she acted.

passage:
In their Ludhiana flat, Baljeet, fifteen, came home from school and threw his bag on the floor. His sister Kalyani was watching TV.
“Change it,” he said.
“I'm watching.”
He grabbed the remote. She pulled it back. He shouted something he didn't even mean.
Kalyani stared at him, then turned away.
Baljeet's chest was tight. He didn't know why he was so angry. Nothing had even happened at school.
He walked out to the park and did three rounds of the track, fast. The anger drained slowly.
When he came back, he sat next to Kalyani. “Sorry. I don't know what's wrong with me lately.”
She shrugged, and handed him the remote. “Your turn.”

qa.q: Where did Baljeet go to calm down?
qa.a: He walked out to the park and did three rounds of the track.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel after shouting at Kalyani?
qa.a: He felt tense and confused, angry for no clear reason.

qa.q: What helped Baljeet choose a better way to act?
qa.a: Going for a fast walk let the anger drain, so he could come back and apologise.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel when Baljeet shouted?
qa.a: She felt hurt and turned away from him.

grounding: A fifteen-year-old notices sudden irritability and chooses to calm down and apologise.

passage:
The door slammed so hard the pictures rattled.
Pradeep knocked a few minutes later. “Parul? Can I come in?”
“Whatever.”
He sat on the edge of her desk chair. “You want to tell me what happened?”
“Nothing happened. That's the problem. I'm just… angry. At everything. Then I want to cry.”
Pradeep nodded slowly. “At your age, moods can swing fast. Your body's changing a lot.”
“So it's not my fault?”
“The feeling isn't. What you do with it is up to you. Slamming doors, or telling me like now.”
Parul picked at the blanket. “Sorry about the door.”
“The door will live. Want to go get chai?”

qa.q: What did Parul do before Pradeep knocked?
qa.a: She slammed the door so hard the pictures rattled.

qa.q: How did Parul feel before talking to her father?
qa.a: She felt angry at everything and like crying, without knowing why.

qa.q: What did Pradeep explain that helped Parul?
qa.a: That moods can swing fast at her age, and while the feeling isn't her fault, she can choose what to do with it.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel after Parul apologises?
qa.a: He probably feels relieved and close to her, glad she talked instead of shutting him out.

grounding: A father helps his sixteen-year-old understand mood shifts and choose how to act on them.

passage:
When I was fifteen, I'd wake up fine, and by lunch I'd want to throw my tiffin at the wall. No reason. Just rage.
One day Gurpreet, my best friend, asked if I wanted to share her samosa. I snapped, "Can you not talk to me for five minutes?" She looked like I'd slapped her.
I felt awful. The mood was still there, buzzing. But I thought: she didn't do anything wrong.
At the end of the day, I walked up to her. "Sorry. I'm in a weird mood and I took it out on you."
She said, "Next time, just say 'weird mood' and I'll give you space." It became our code.
I'm Naveen. The moods still come sometimes. But now I don't let them do the talking.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet offer to share?
qa.a: Her samosa.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling after snapping at Gurpreet?
qa.a: Naveen felt awful and guilty, knowing Gurpreet hadn't done anything wrong.

qa.q: What did Naveen do after snapping that others could copy?
qa.a: Naveen apologised, explained the mood without blaming Gurpreet, and agreed on a code for next time.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet feel when Naveen apologises?
qa.a: Gurpreet likely feels relieved and understood, and willing to give space next time.

grounding: A young person recalls sudden teenage irritability and learning to act well despite it.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 9.
Shreya has been short-tempered this week. On Monday she slammed her book when a classmate borrowed her pen. On Wednesday she cried in the washroom, then came back and laughed as if nothing happened.
Today I asked her to stay after class. She said, "I don't know why. One minute I'm fine, then I'm angry at everyone."
I told her mood swings are common at this age, and that it doesn't make her a bad person. We talked about noticing the mood early. She said a walk to the water cooler helps. I told her she may step out for a minute if she needs to.
I'll check in with her on Monday. — Parveen Siddiqui

qa.q: What did Shreya slam on Monday?
qa.a: Her book.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling when she said "I don't know why"?
qa.a: Shreya felt confused and frustrated by her own sudden moods.

qa.q: What did Parveen Siddiqui offer that could help Shreya manage her moods?
qa.a: Permission to step out for a minute, and the idea of noticing the mood early and using a short walk.

qa.q: How might Shreya's classmates be affected by the new plan?
qa.a: They may get fewer sharp reactions, since Shreya can step away before she snaps.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teen understanding her mood swings and choosing how to act.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today was a mess. I woke up irritated for NO reason. Then Noor texted "hey 😊" and I replied "what" like a total grump.
She didn't reply for an hour. I felt worse.
Then Ammi asked me to bring the washing in and I rolled my eyes so hard. I know she saw.
In the evening I sat on the terrace and thought: I can't control the mood, but I can control what I say. So I texted Noor: "Sorry, I was rude. Weird mood, not you." She sent back a hug.
Then I brought Ammi tea without being asked. She raised an eyebrow and smiled.
Tomorrow, if the mood comes, I'll count to five before replying.
— Nirmala

qa.q: What did Noor text?
qa.a: "hey 😊"

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling when Noor didn't reply for an hour?
qa.a: Nirmala felt worse, guilty and anxious about being rude.

qa.q: What did Nirmala decide to try tomorrow if the mood comes?
qa.a: Counting to five before replying, so the mood doesn't control what Nirmala says.

qa.q: How might Ammi see the tea Nirmala brought?
qa.a: Ammi probably sees it as a quiet apology and is pleased 😊.

grounding: In a diary a teen notices sudden irritability and chooses to repair and act differently.

passage:
In their small town near the river, Chinmay came home from tuition and slammed the door so hard the calendar fell. His sister Shreya, doing homework on the floor, looked up.
"What happened?"
"Nothing! Why does everyone keep asking?"
She went back to her book. He stood in the middle of the room, breathing hard. Nothing had happened. That was the strange part. He just felt like everything was too loud and too close.
He grabbed his cycle and rode to the ghat. He sat watching the boats for twenty minutes until his chest stopped feeling tight.
When he came back, he picked up the calendar and hung it up again. "Sorry, Shreya. It's not you. I'm just… cranky all the time lately."
She shrugged. "You were like a pressure cooker."

qa.q: Where did Chinmay ride to?
qa.a: Chinmay rode his cycle to the ghat.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay feel confused about his anger?
qa.a: Chinmay felt irritable and overwhelmed even though nothing had actually happened, which confused him.

qa.q: Which choice helped Chinmay, and why?
qa.a: Riding to the ghat to calm down before talking helped, because he could apologise once his chest stopped feeling tight.

qa.q: How might Shreya see her brother's moods?
qa.a: Shreya seems a little wary but understanding, joking that he was like a pressure cooker once he apologised.

grounding: Shows a teen experiencing a sudden unexplained mood, taking space and choosing to apologise.

passage:
Ingrid burst into tears in the Stockholm café because Clara took the last cinnamon bun. The actual last bun. She was mortified even as it happened.
"Okay," Clara said slowly, pushing the plate over. "This isn't about a bun."
"I don't know what it's about," Ingrid said, wiping her face with a napkin. "I was fine this morning. Then Mamma asked about my test and I wanted to scream at her."
"Did you?"
"No. I said I'd talk after school. I went to my room first."
"That's good, right?"
Ingrid nodded. She took a breath. "I think I'll text her now that I was grumpy, not angry at her. And then talk about the test tonight, when I'm not crying over bread."
Clara laughed. "Want half?"

qa.q: What did Clara take that set Ingrid off?
qa.a: Clara took the last cinnamon bun.

qa.q: How did Ingrid feel after bursting into tears?
qa.a: Ingrid was mortified and confused, not knowing why the mood had hit so hard.

qa.q: What did Ingrid do well in handling her mood with her mother?
qa.a: Ingrid put off the talk and went to her room instead of screaming, and plans to explain and have the talk once she feels calmer.

qa.q: How might Clara see Ingrid's outburst?
qa.a: Clara seems patient and a bit amused, understanding that the tears aren't really about the bun.

grounding: Illustrates a teen understanding a sudden mood and choosing how to act with her mother despite it.

passage:
In the Class 9 science lab, Farida's test tube cracked. Pradeep, her lab partner, said, "Careful, you'll break everything."
"Maybe if you did something instead of watching!" Farida snapped, loud enough for the whole row to hear.
Pradeep went quiet. Farida's face burned. She didn't know why she was so angry. Yesterday she'd cried at a movie and this morning she'd shouted at her little brother over a sock.
At break, she sat on the stairs alone. The biology teacher passing by stopped. "Rough day?"
"I keep getting angry for nothing, Ma'am."
"Moods can swing a lot at your age. That's normal. But you still get to choose what you do next."
After break, Farida found Pradeep at the tap. "Sorry. That was about me, not you."
Pradeep shrugged, then smiled. "I was watching too much, though."

qa.q: What happened to Farida's test tube?
qa.a: Farida's test tube cracked.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling after snapping at Pradeep?
qa.a: Farida felt embarrassed and confused, her face burning, not understanding why she was so angry.

qa.q: What did the teacher's words help Farida do?
qa.a: They helped her see that moods can swing at her age but she can still choose her actions, so she went and apologised.

qa.q: How does Pradeep respond to Farida's apology?
qa.a: Pradeep accepts it easily, even admitting his own part, which shows he wasn't holding a grudge.

grounding: Shows a teenager noticing sudden mood swings and choosing to apologise instead of letting the mood decide.
